purpose: Explain in very simple language how many clear cloud droplets redirect mixed-color sunlight into a diffuse white glow, while a thick cloud base receives less light and can look grey.
title: A crowd of clear drops makes a white cloud
story: Sunlight arrives as many visible colors together.
Clear water droplets, each much larger than a visible-light wave, redirect the colors with similar overall strength.
Inside a crowd of droplets, light changes direction many times and escapes in many directions as a mixed white glow.
In a thick cloud, less light reaches the bottom, so the base can look grey even though the droplets remain clear.
observed: Warm-cloud droplets measured in situ have a typical radius near 11 micrometres, many times larger than visible-light wavelengths.
Cloud optical thickness changes strongly with liquid-water amount and droplet size.
Cloud brightness and inferred optical thickness vary with three-dimensional shape, sun angle, and viewing angle.
inferred: The drawn light paths are a teaching schematic, not tracks of measured individual photons; keep them thin, simple, and clearly representative.
Do not imply that every color follows an identical route or that water droplets absorb most visible light.
layout_notes: Use one continuous left-to-right scientific mechanism on a white 3:2 landscape canvas, with three lower-case labeled regions rather than boxed cards.
At left, show three thin parallel red, green, and blue rays grouped as incoming sunlight; they enter a large central cross-section of a pale cloud.
Build the cloud from many small transparent, outlined spherical water droplets. Show several thin light paths changing direction between droplets without clutter.

At right and upper edges, show neutral pale rays leaving in several directions as the white glow. At the bottom, use a restrained light-grey shaded region and fewer rays to show that less light arrives there.
Place every label in quiet white space with a short thin leader. Keep the reading order obvious at phone width.
constraints: Arial throughout, with all labels at least 20 px at a 1536 px canvas width.
Depict each droplet as clear water, never as an opaque white ball, soap bubble, snowball, or raindrop shape.
Use colored rays only to introduce the mixed colors in sunlight. After repeated redirects, use neutral white-to-pale-grey rays rather than a rainbow.
Every arrow or ray must represent incoming sunlight, a change in direction, escape from the cloud, or reduced light at the base.
Keep the bottom label visible and do not imply that grey droplets cause the shaded base.
